newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. threatens sanctions against Angola's UNITA.
newsitem.headline: U.N. threatens sanctions against Angola's UNITA.

text.p: The Security Council on Friday threatened sanctions against Angola's former rebel UNITA movement and extended the U.N.'s 7,200-strong peacekeeping mission there for two months only.

But the 15-member body turned down demands from southern African countries to automatically begin sanctions next month unless UNITA (the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) complied with peace accords that ended two decades of civil warfare.

Instead, the resolution, drafted by the United States, Russia and Portugal, says the council would consider bans against UNITA's trade in the oil- and mineral-rich country if no progress has been made by Nov. 20.
This could also include freezing bank accounts abroad and the prevention of travel unless Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali reports "substantial and genuine progress."
The council threatened such actions in September 1993 but never instituted them. It has imposed an oil and arms embargo against UNITA but has had trouble enforcing it.

In its resolution, the council called on UNITA, once backed by white South Africa and the United States, to comply with 12 different demands and expressed "deep disappointment" at UNITA's refusal to institute the agreements it signed.

The United Nations says UNITA has delayed integrating 26,000 fighters into a national army with its former enemies, interfered with U.N. peacekeepers and helicopters deployed in its key areas, and relinquished only old arms for those guerrillas being demobilized.

The United Nations' peacekeeping operation in Angola, its largest remaining mission, will be renewed for two months until Dec. 20, in order to maintain pressure on both parties. But the mission is expected to be renewed until at least Feb. 8, the target date for ending the operation altogether.
The United Nations is helping to implement an agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in November 1994 that ends nearly 20 years of civil war between the Angolan government and UNITA.

Jonas Savimbi, UNITA's leader, snubbed his southern African neighbours earlier this month at a summit they organised to break the deadlock in Angola. He has also rejected the vice presidency reserved for him under the peace accord, in part because it would have meant moving away from his base to government-held Luanda which he mistrusts.

During the Cold War, UNITA forces were bolstered by those from South Africa's apartheid government with the acquiescence of the United States while its opponents were helped by Cuban troops backed by the then-Soviet Union.

In a day-long debate on Thursday, the foreign ministers of Zimbabwe, Angola, Mozambique and Botswana, as well as envoys of other African nations, pressed the council to take definitive action. They expressed alarm that war might break out in Angola again, thereby destabilising the region.

"The council must send a clear unambiguous message to UNITA: Time is up, the game is over," said Zimbabwe's Foreign Minister Stanislaus Mudenge. "Apparently scheming, selfishness, greed and self-aggrandizement have stymied the peace process."
